fetched_contents.text: The utilization of Ricinus communis in the phytomanagement of heavy metal contaminated soils Publication: Environmental Reviews 7 July 2020 Abstract Soil contamination with toxic metals is a major global concern due to their effects on plants and the ecosystem. In contaminated soils, some plant species have the ability to remediate heavy metals. Ricinus communis L., is an industrial crop plant gaining popularity in the remediation of heavy metal contaminated soils owing to its strong and deep penetrating roots aiding high metal accumulation and large biomass level. Ricinus communis can tolerate high amounts of metals by adopting different strategies, which include the production of antioxidant enzymes, subcellular localization, and exudation of organic acid. At the molecular level, R. communis can tolerate metal stress by activating stress-responsive genes. Proper selection of metal-tolerant R. communis cultivars is effective in the remediation of metal-contaminated soils, owing to their high capacity for metal tolerance. Exogenous application of mineral fertilization and the use of microbes and chelating agents increase metal solubility and availability for plant uptake in soil. Also, good agronomic practices such as co-planting of R. communis with other leguminous crops enhance R. communis growth and metal tolerance, thereby improving remediation of metal-contaminated soils. This review, therefore, critically discusses the recent approaches in using R. communis to remediate metal-contaminated soils. Résumé La contamination du sol par des métaux toxiques est une préoccupation majeure à l’échelle planétaire en raison de leurs effets sur les plantes et l’écosystème. Dans les sols contaminés, certaines espèces végétales ont la capacité d’éliminer les métaux lourds. Ricinus communis L. est une plante cultivée de manière industrielle qui gagne en popularité dans l’assainissement des sols contaminés par les métaux lourds grâce à ses racines robustes et profondes qui favorisent une forte accumulation de métaux et un niveau élevé de biomasse. Ricinus communis peut tolérer de grandes quantités de métaux en adoptant différentes stratégies qui comprennent la production d’enzymes antioxydantes, la localisation subcellulaire et l’exsudation d’acides organiques. À l’échelle moléculaire, R. communis peut tolérer le stress provoqué par les métaux en activant des gènes sensibles au stress. Une sélection appropriée de cultivars de R. communis tolérants aux métaux est efficace pour l’assainissement de sols contaminés par les métaux, en raison de leur grande capacité de tolérance aux métaux. L’application exogène de fertilisation minérale et l’utilisation de microbes et d’agents chélateurs accroissent la solubilité et la disponibilité des métaux pour leur absorption par les plantes dans le sol. Par ailleurs, de bonnes pratiques agronomiques comme la coplantation de R. communis avec d’autres cultures de légumineuses augmentent la croissance et la tolérance aux métaux de R. communis, améliorant ainsi l’assainissement des sols contaminés par les métaux. Cette synthèse examine donc de manière critique les approches récentes de l’utilisation de R. communis pour assainir les sols contaminés par les métaux. [Traduit par la Rédaction] 1. Introduction Elements with densities above 5 g·cm−3 are known as heavy metals. Among the metallic elements that occur, over 50 elements form part of the heavy metal group (Alloway 2013). Some of these metals, which may promote plant growth and development, are essential. Among such metals are copper (Cu), manganese (Mn), molybdenum (Mo), iron (Fe), and zinc (Zn). Another category of these metals that includes cadmium (Cd), nickel (Ni), and lead (Pb) are toxic even at low levels. Generally, these metals are present in the soil but in low quantities; however, natural phenomena (e.g., volcanic eruption, weathering, and soil erosion) and anthropogenic and industrial activities (e.g., mining, phosphate fertilizer, sewage sludge, coal burning, petroleum combustion, and textiles) have led to higher concentrations of these metals in the atmosphere (Alloway 2012; Zhu et al. 2019). During intense rainfall, these metals enter the soil, making agricultural soil unfit for use (Jiang et al. 2019). It is quite clear that heavy metals are non-degradable and can persist for a long period of time in soil. Excess exposure to these heavy metals in soil affects plant growth by disrupting photosynthetic pigments, enzymatic reaction, and plant physiology (D’Alessandro et al. 2013; Silva et al. 2017). In addition, heavy metals induce oxidative stress by the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in plants (Mallhi et al. 2019). Heavy metals can affect human health as they enters the food chain through plants that uptake water and mineral nutrients from the contaminated soil. For these reasons, the recovery of metal-contaminated soil would be beneficial for agricultural purposes. Phytomanagement (biofortification, phytomining, and phytoremediation) of metal-contaminated soils involves the utilization of vegetation for alleviating any environmental risk related with the site in a cost-effective manner (Gómez-Sagasti et al. 2018). The techniques involved in phytomanagement of metal soils are aesthetically acceptable, economical, and eco-friendly. Phytoextraction as part of phytoremediation techniques employs the use of plant species to clean metal-contaminated soils by accumulating metals in the plant system (roots and shoots). The fate and success of phytoextraction are largely based on the type of plant species that can tolerate metal accumulation. Several plant species have been suggested for phytoremediation of metal-contaminated soils (Shakoor et al. 2017). Ricinus communis L., a non-edible oilseed crop known as castor belonging to the family Euphorbiaceace, is widely grown in many countries, with India, China, and Brazil contributing about 90% of the world’s production (Sbihi et al. 2018). Growth in single element or co-contaminated soils: Pot experiments Abstract Using biofuel plants to remove metal pollutants is a sustainable approach for phytoremediation. Ricinus communis L. (castor bean) is a bioenergy plant that grows rapidly and has a high biomass; it has been proven to be a potential phytoaccumulator of several metals. Pot experiments with single element or co-contaminated soils were conducted to investigate Cd, Cu and Zn accumulation and their interaction in R. communis L. After growing for four months in soils with the addition of Cd (at rates of 1,5,10,20, and 40 mg/kg), Cu (at rates of 50, 100, 200, 400, and 600 mg/kg), and Zn (at rates of 100,200,400,600, and 800 mg/kg) alone or combined, the dry biomass and the concentrations of Cd, Cu, and Zn in the leaves, stems and roots of the castor bean plants were measured, and the translocation and bioaccumulation factors were calculated. It was found that all of the R. communis grew well and produced high biomass, showing a high tolerance to Cd, Cu and Zn. Our experimental results implied that R. communis showed a high phytoremediation potential for soils contaminated by Cd or Zn while displayed a low uptake of Cu. The copper concentration in R. communis was only slightly influenced by Cd and Zn additions to the soils. The interaction pattern of Cd and Zn showed an antagonistic behavior under low concentrations of the Cd and Zn combined treatment while showed a synergistic behavior under high concentrations of the Cd and Zn combined treatment. Introduction In recent years, with the development of industry and wastewater irrigation, an increasing amount of heavy metals (HMs) has entered the soil environment. The heavy metals can cause great harm to human health and the environment due to their high occurrence as a contaminant, low solubility in biota, and possible carcinogenicity (Diels et al., 2002). The removal of heavy metals from contaminated soils has become an urgent issue. Phytoremediation, which is defined as the use of plants to remove contaminants from contaminated soils, has attracted extensive attention because it is an economical, environment friendly and aesthetically acceptable approach (Bauddh and Singh, 2012, Lakshmi et al., 2013). However, this technology is limited because the known hyperaccumulator plants are rare herbs with small biomass, which have little economic value (Linger et al., 2002, Chen et al., 2012). A new strategy of using energy crops to accumulate HMs from contaminated soils has been suggested, which can help to solve two critical global problems, namely, the gradual reduction of fossil fuels and soil contamination (Ruiz Olivares et al., 2013). Ricinus communis L. is a bioenergy plant that grows rapidly and has a high biomass. It has been shown that R. communis has the potential to tolerate and extract heavy metals, such as Cd (Bauddh and Singh, 2012), As (Melo et al., 2009), Ni (Adhikari and Kumar, 2012), and Cu (Andreazza et al., 2013). Recently, there has been increased interest in this plant because of its high economic value. The oil content of the R. communis seed can reach 70% (Vamerali et al., 2010). R. communis is well adapted to salinity, drought, and frost and does not require special soil conditions (Sipos et al., 2013). Moreover, castor plant is an industrial crop and cannot enter the food cycle (Rajkumar and Freitas, 2008). Soil pollution by heavy metals is typically not limited to a single element; several metals may be present in high concentrations in soils (Marchiol et al., 2004). Interactions among metals, including antagonistic, additive and synergistic effects, may influence HM uptake and transport in plants. The addition of Zn to soils led to a suppression of Cd accumulation in the aboveground parts of Matricaria recutita (Chizzola and Mitteregger, 2005). In contrast, the absorption of Cd by rice was promoted because of the addition of Zn (Zhou et al., 2003). However, the effects of the interactions between heavy metals on R. communis growth and metal accumulation have not been reported. The goals of this study were the following: (1) to evaluate the Cd, Cu and Zn tolerance and accumulation capacity of R. communis under single element or multi-contaminated conditions; (2) to address the interactive effects of Cd, Cu and Zn on the R. communis soil system. fetched_contents.text: Medicago sativa L. enhances the phytoextraction of cadmium and zinc by Ricinus communis L. on contaminated land in situ Abstract Crop co-planting is widely used in agriculture because it can increase total crop yields through increased resource use efficiency, and phytoremediation is based on the contaminant remediation system in plants. This study focused on the phytoextractive effects of co-planting Ricinus communis and/or legumes in Cd- and Zn-contaminated soil. A Cd- and Zn-contaminated factory relocation site in Shanghai was selected for the experiment, and according to the results of a potential ecological risk assessment of heavy metals, the study area was divided into 3 levels of pollution: slight, moderate, and high. The results showed that the presence of Medicago sativa can significantly increase the height and biomass of R. communis, and there was a greater impact on the chlorophyll content of R. communis at higher pollution levels. Differences in pollution levels could significantly change the oil content of R. communis plants, but M. sativa can alleviate the impact of heavy metals. The presence of M. sativa increased the cumulative amount of cadmium and zinc in R. communis by 1.14 and 2.19 times, respectively. In short, co-planting R. communis and legumes remediated contaminated soil and may be one practical phytoremediation pathway for heavy metal-contaminated soil in the future. Introduction As the world has undergone industrial economic growth, heavy metals have gradually accumulated in agricultural soils. It is said that more than 16.1% of soils in China are contaminated, including 7.0% with cadmium (Cd) and 0.9% with zinc (Zn) (Chen et al., 2016). Therefore, the remediation of contaminated soil is necessary to save land resources and protect human health (Kramer, 2005, Vangronsveld et al., 2009). Phytoremediation is based on the contaminant remediation system in plants, and it has recently become an economically, environmentally and aesthetically accepted technology (Ahmadpour et al., 2012, Conventionally, 2011, Majid et al., 2012). Ricinus communis L. is an oilseed crop in the Euphorbiaceae family (Wale and Assegie, 2015) that has a high biomass and a well-developed root system. China produces the second largest amount of R. communis in the world (Bauddh and Singh, 2015), and the crop is also metal tolerant, with a high tolerance to Cd concentrations (Shi and Cai, 2009). R. communis has a higher remediation efficiency than Indian mustard (Brassica juncea L.), which is considered a potential phytoremediator (Bauddh and Singh, 2012), and it has a high phytoremediation potential for cadmium- and zinc-contaminated soils (Wang et al., 2016). However, fast-growing and high biomass plants often contain low to moderate concentrations of heavy metals (McGrath et al., 2001). Thus, researchers have studied several approaches to improve the potential for heavy metal phytoextraction using R. communis. One idea was to apply metal chelators, but some chemical chelators are relatively expensive and present environmental risks (Wu et al., 2006). In addition, a low concentration of chemical chelators can reduce plant biomass (Chen and Cutright, 2001). Furthermore, plants can increase metal bioavailability by themselves; experiments have shown that some plant roots can produce H+ and small-molecular-weight organic acids that can increase the amount of bioavailable metals (Duarte et al., 2007). Crop co-planting has been widely used in agriculture in China for 2000 years (Zhang and Li, 2003), and legumes are often included in such systems because of their ability to fix N2 (Karpenstein-Machan and Stuelpnagel, 2000, van Kessel and Hartley, 2000). In this study, we assumed that N-fixers can provide additional N to the main crop plant, which can produce substantial biomass and thus enhance the phytoextraction of cadmium and zinc from contaminated soil. We used Medicago sativa L. as the legume species to intercrop with R. communis because it is a metal-tolerant plant that can tolerate both zinc and cadmium (Desjardins et al., 2016, Kabir et al., 2016). We focused on the phytoextraction of cadmium and zinc from contaminated soil, and our main objectives were to investigate (i) whether co-planting with the legume affected the chlorophyll and oil contents of R. communis, (ii) whether co-planting with the legume affected the growth and biomass of the phytoextractor (R. communis), and (iii) whether co-planting with the legume enhanced the phytoextraction of cadmium and zinc by R. communis. fetched_contents.text: Cadmium and zinc interactions and their transfer in soil-crop system under actual field conditions Abstract The transfer of Cd and Zn from calcareous soils nearby a non-ferrous mining and smelting bases to the spring wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) and corn (Zea mays L.) tissues and the interactions between the two metals concerned were investigated under actual field conditions. Samples of soils and entire crops were randomly collected during harvest time in 1998 in the Baiyin region. The soil metal contents showed that the furrows had been polluted (mean values: 3.16 mg kg−1 for Cd; 146.78 mg kg−1 for Zn) and the significant spatial variation of the soil contamination existed here (ranges, Cd: 0.14–19.3 mg kg−1; Zn: 43.5–565.0 mg kg−1). The translocation ratios of the two metals from soil to crop parts in the region studied were relatively lower and the order of the element transfer in different plant tissues was root>stem>grain. The transfer ratio of element Cd was lower than that of element Zn. Cd and Zn uptake by the crop structures could be best described by four models (P<0.01): linear; exponential; quadratic; and cubic. Apart from a linear relationship between the element Cd in the corn grains and soils, models were generally non-linear. An analysis of CdZn interaction mechanism led to the conclusion that the effects of the two metals were synergistic to each other under field conditions, in which increasing Cd and Zn contents in soils could increase the accumulations of Zn or Cd in the two crops. Introduction Toxic heavy metal contamination in soils and crop plants is of major importance due to their health effects on humans and other animals (Farmer and Farmer, 2000, Pichtel et al., 2000). Cadmium (Cd) is a toxic element and zinc (Zn) is toxic in high concentrations, and numerous investigations showed that the pronounced amounts of Cd and Zn were often found in arable soils adjacent to a non-ferrous metal production bases (Pierzynski and Schwab, 1993, Dudka et al., 1996, Dahmani-Muller et al., 2000). The processing and subsequent release of zinc to the environment is normally accompanied by cadmium environmental pollution because of zinc ores (ZnS) generally containing 0.1–5% and sometimes even higher cadmium (Adriano, 1986). The trace elements concerned entered the soils mainly from sludge-borne heavy metal applications and industrial wastewater irrigation, and partially from aerial deposition and the usage of fertilizers and pesticides (Mench et al., 1994, Ullrich et al., 1999, Nan and Zhao, 2000, Sterckeman et al., 2000). Heavy metal uptake by roots depends on both soil and crop plant factors (e.g. source and chemical form of elements in soil, pH, CEC, organic material, plant species and tissues, plant age, etc.). Interactions among the co-exist elements occurring at root surface and within the plant also affect uptake and translocation. Cadmium, unessential to plants, and zinc, essential to plants, are elements having similar geochemical and environmental properties. This association of cadmium and zinc in the environment and their chemical similarity can lead to interaction between cadmium and zinc during plant uptake, transport from roots to aboveground parts, or accumulation in edible parts (Das et al., 1997). Accumulation of heavy metals in crop tissues and transfer of them in soil crop system had well been documented (Dudka et al., 1996, Barman et al., 2000, Kisku et al., 2000). Interactions of Cd and Zn and their accumulation in plant parts in solution culture or in pot experiment had been reported (Coughtrey and Martin, 1979, Smilde et al., 1992, Moraghan, 1993, Mckenna et al., 1993, Dudka et al., 1994, Zhou et al., 1994). However, to our knowledge, there is little information about the fates and behaviors of the metals in crop tissues in fields. Therefore, the present investigation was undertaken to examine the interactions between cadmium and zinc in arable soils and their effects on the accumulation of both metals in crop structures. Spring wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) and corn (Zea mays L.) were chosen because they are staples in the diet of the local people in the northern China, and both of the crops readily absorb Cd and Zn from ZnCd contaminated soils (Hinsely et al., 1984, Dudka et al., 1994). The goals of our study were to examine in these two crops: (1) distribution patterns of cadmium and zinc contents in different parts of the two crops grown in the field influenced by non-ferrous metal mining and smelting operation; (2) transfer ratios and relationship models of the two metals concerned from soils to plant parts; and (3) effects of CdZn interactions on the concentrations of both metals in crop tissues. Mechanisms explaining changes in Ricinus communis growth when co-planted with legumes are shaped by both direct resource interactions and soil-level chemistry. The evidence suggests that legumes can improve Ricinus growth through nutrient availability and resource facilitation rather than pure allelopathy. In the co-planting review evidence, Ricinus is described as a crop that benefits from good agronomic practices such as co-planting with other leguminous crops, which enhances growth and metal tolerance [N1-F1]. This implies that legumes may improve Ricinus growth by optimizing resource use rather than by antagonistic competition.

The legume-related evidence also shows that legumes can alter competitive dynamics through nitrogen fixation and other root interactions. The cited review on legumes in intercropping systems notes that allelopathy can act as a protectant, defense, and growth stimulant, but the evidence here is general rather than specific to Ricinus [N5-R4]. More directly, studies on Ricinus allelopathy indicate that aqueous extracts can inhibit seed germination and growth, but the same evidence also shows that some concentrations may promote shoot growth while inhibiting root growth [N5-R2][N5-R5]. This is important because it shows that the dominant interaction can shift depending on the plant part and extract concentration; Ricinus may sometimes exert inhibitory allelopathy, but legumes may more often provide facilitative effects through nitrogen fixation and root architecture.

Root architecture and mycorrhizal associations are not explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, so those mechanisms must be treated as plausible but not directly confirmed. The legume evidence is strongest on competitive and allelopathic interactions, while the soil-chemistry context emphasizes how metal availability and soil amendments influence plant uptake and root function [N4-F4]. That context is useful for explaining why co-planting may indirectly affect root architecture: legumes can change soil pH, organic matter, and metal bioavailability, which in turn affect root morphology and nutrient uptake. The review on Cd/Zn interactions and transfer also notes that metal availability is influenced by pH, organic matter, and other soil factors [N4-F4]. Therefore, the strongest explanation in the evidence is that legumes improve Ricinus growth mainly by enhancing nutrient availability, reducing competitive stress, and altering soil chemistry rather than through a single dominant allelopathic effect [N1-F1][N5-R4][N4-F4].

Biomass and shoot/root ratios also appear to be affected by co-planting. The direct co-planting study on Medicago sativa and Ricinus communis reports that M. sativa significantly increased the height and biomass of R. communis, and that this effect was especially evident at higher pollution levels [N3-F3]. It also notes that biomass changes were associated with differences in pollution levels, but M. sativa alleviated the impact of heavy metals [N3-F3]. The evidence does not provide a shoot/root ratio specifically, but it does show that co-planting can increase biomass, suggesting a more favorable biomass allocation than monocultures [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports a facilitative pattern in which legumes improve Ricinus growth through nutrient facilitation, reduced competitive stress, and improved metal tolerance, with allelopathy present only as a potential secondary or context-dependent factor [N1-F1][N5-R4][N5-R2][N4-F4].
node_outputs.N9:
Medicago sativa plays a supportive role in Cd and Zn phytoremediation by enhancing Ricinus communis growth and metal uptake, but its own direct accumulation or tolerance of Cd and Zn is not the main focus of the provided evidence. The direct study on co-planting M. sativa with R. communis explicitly states that M. sativa significantly increased the height and biomass of R. communis and increased the cumulative Cd and Zn in R. communis by 1.14 and 2.19 times, respectively [N3-F3]. It also reports that M. sativa alleviated the impact of heavy metals, indicating that it can reduce stress rather than merely passively coexist with R. communis [N3-F3]. This makes M. sativa more of a facilitator than a direct accumulator of Cd and Zn in the evidence provided.

The evidence also suggests that M. sativa may improve soil chemistry and metal bioavailability. The study notes that co-planting affected chlorophyll content and that differences in pollution levels changed oil content, but the strongest soil-chemistry implication is that legumes can alter nutrient availability and reduce the negative impact of heavy metals [N3-F3]. The soil-interaction context adds that Cd and Zn availability depends on pH, organic matter, and other soil properties, which implies that legumes can indirectly increase metal bioavailability by modifying soil conditions [N4-F4]. However, the provided evidence does not show that M. sativa itself greatly accumulates Cd and Zn; instead, it appears to enhance R. communis’s uptake and reduce the stress burden on R. communis [N3-F3][N4-F4].

Regarding whether M. sativa enhances or inhibits Cd/Zn uptake by Ricinus, the evidence strongly supports enhancement. The co-planting study reports increased Cd and Zn in R. communis when M. sativa was present [N3-F3]. The review evidence also states that legumes can improve resource use efficiency and that good agronomic practices such as co-planting can enhance growth and metal tolerance [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence suggests facilitative enhancement rather than inhibition. The role of M. sativa in soil chemistry is therefore primarily indirect: it may alter nutrient availability, reduce metal toxicity, and improve the conditions under which R. communis accumulates Cd and Zn [N3-F3][N1-F1][N4-F4].

On biomass and growth responses, the evidence is clear. M. sativa significantly increased the height and biomass of R. communis, and there was a greater impact on chlorophyll content at higher pollution levels [N3-F3]. The branch reports emphasize that Cd and Zn contamination changes plant-soil interactions by altering metal availability and soil chemistry. The soil-context evidence states that Cd and Zn availability is influenced by pH, organic matter, and other soil properties, which are important for plant uptake and root function [N4-F4]. The Cd/Zn interaction review also notes that the two metals can interact during uptake, transport, and accumulation, supporting the idea that soil chemistry mediates plant responses [N4-F4]. In the Ricinus study, the plant is described as a heavy-metal-tolerant species that can grow well and produce high biomass under Cd, Cu, and Zn contamination, but growth was reduced at higher Cd concentrations [N2-F2]. This shows that Cd and Zn contamination can impair growth, even in a tolerant species, and that the severity of the effect depends on the concentration and combination of metals [N2-F2][N4-F4].

The legume evidence also shows that legumes can alter competitive dynamics and resource availability. The intercropping review notes that allelopathy can act as a protectant, defense, and growth stimulant, but the evidence is general rather than specific to Ricinus [N5-R4]. More directly, studies on Ricinus allelopathy indicate that aqueous extracts can inhibit germination and growth, while some concentrations may promote shoot growth while inhibiting root growth [N5-R2][N5-R5]. This suggests that legumes may reduce competitive stress and improve resource use, but the exact direction depends on plant-part responses and extract concentration [N5-R4][N5-R2][N5-R5].

### 4) What role Medicago sativa plays in Cd and Zn phytoremediation

Medicago sativa appears to act as a facilitator rather than a direct accumulator of Cd and Zn in the provided evidence. The co-planting study shows that M. sativa significantly increased the height and biomass of R. communis and increased Cd and Zn uptake by R. communis by 1.14 and 2.19 times, respectively [N3-F3]. It also reports that M. sativa alleviated the impact of heavy metals, indicating that it can reduce stress rather than merely coexist with R. communis [N3-F3]. This makes M. sativa a supportive phytoremediation partner, especially for Cd and Zn-contaminated soils.

The evidence also suggests that M. sativa may improve soil chemistry and metal bioavailability. The study notes that co-planting affected chlorophyll content and that differences in pollution levels changed oil content, but the strongest soil-chemistry implication is that legumes can alter nutrient availability and reduce the negative impact of heavy metals [N3-F3]. The soil-interaction context adds that Cd and Zn availability depends on pH, organic matter, and other soil properties, implying that legumes can indirectly increase metal bioavailability by modifying soil conditions [N4-F4]. However, the provided evidence does not show that M. sativa itself greatly accumulates Cd and Zn; instead, it appears to enhance R. communis’s uptake and reduce the stress burden on R. communis [N3-F3][N1-F1][N4-F4].

### 5) How soil contamination levels and study designs matter

The most relevant study designs are primarily pot and field experiments, with Cd and Zn concentrations varying across studies. The Ricinus study used pot experiments with single-element or co-contaminated soils, adding Cd at 1, 5, 10, 20, and 40 mg/kg, Cu at 50, 100, 200, 400, and 600 mg/kg, and Zn at 100, 200, 400, 600, and 800 mg/kg [N2-F2]. It also reports that Cd, Cu, and Zn concentrations in the experimental soil were 0.13, 21.4, and 74.6 mg/kg, respectively [N2-F2]. The Cd/Zn interaction field study found furrow soil Cd at 3.16 mg/kg and Zn at 146.78 mg/kg, with ranges of Cd: 0.14–19.3 mg/kg and Zn: 43.5–565.0 mg/kg [N4-F4]. These levels indicate that the studies cover both low-to-moderate and higher contamination contexts [N2-F2][N4-F4].

Most studies used single-species or co-planting/mixed-cropping designs rather than random natural communities. The Ricinus study used pot experiments with single-element or co-contaminated soils [N2-F2]. The M. sativa co-planting study used field co-planting of R. communis and M. sativa in a Cd- and Zn-contaminated factory relocation site [N3-F3]. The Cd/Zn interaction study used spring wheat and corn in a Cd- and Zn-contaminated area [N4-F4]. This means the evidence is built around controlled, manipulative experiments rather than purely observational field surveys [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4].

Soil types and amendments tested vary across the studies. The Ricinus study used soil collected from the surface layer of farmland in Beijing, China, and the experimental soil was mixed with appropriate amounts of R. communis growth and biomass material [N2-F2]. The Cd/Zn interaction study was conducted in a calcareous soil region near a non-ferrous mining and smelting base in northern China [N4-F4]. The amendments evidence adds that biochar, compost, and peat can change available Cd and Zn, with biochar immobilizing Cd and Zn while compost and peat increasing their availability [N6-R1]. It also notes that phosphates, manures, and biochars reduce heavy-metal solubility through precipitation, adsorption, and other mechanisms [N6-R2]. This indicates that the relevant contamination contexts include calcareous soils, farmland soils, and soils amended with organic or mineral materials [N2-F2][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2].

Control of metal interactions and amendments is unevenly documented in the provided evidence. The Ricinus study explicitly reports single-element and co-contaminated treatments and calculates interaction patterns, showing that Cd and Zn can behave antagonistically or synergistically depending on concentration [N2-F2]. The Cd/Zn interaction study also examines interactions in the field and reports that Cd and Zn can interact during uptake, transport, and accumulation [N4-F4]. However, the amendments evidence shows that amendments can change metal availability, but it is not clear from the provided excerpts whether every study controlled for all amendment types or whether all interactions were explicitly measured [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Overall, the most relevant designs are pot and field experiments with single-species or co-planting/mixed-cropping, covering Cd and Zn concentrations from low to high and including soil amendments that alter metal availability [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2].

### 6) Soil amendments and Cd/Zn uptake

Soil amendments can enhance metal uptake by increasing solubility and availability. The Ricinus study notes that exogenous application of mineral fertilization, microbes, and chelating agents increases metal solubility and availability for plant uptake in soil [N1-F1]. It also found that R. communis showed high phytoremediation potential for Cd or Zn while displaying low uptake of Cu [N2-F2]. This implies that soil amendments can improve metal bioavailability and uptake, but the response is crop-specific. The soil-interaction context adds that Cd and Zn availability is influenced by pH, organic matter, and other soil properties [N4-F4], which supports the idea that amendments can change metal availability and therefore uptake [N4-F4][N1-F1].

Cd and Zn interact during uptake and plant responses in a concentration-dependent manner. The Ricinus study reports that Cd and Zn showed antagonistic behavior under low concentrations and synergistic behavior under high concentrations [N2-F2]. The Cd/Zn interaction review also states that the two metals can interact during uptake, transport, and accumulation [N4-F4]. This means Cd and Zn do not act independently; their combined presence can either reduce or amplify uptake, depending on concentration and context [N2-F2][N4-F4].

### 7) Practical implications

The practical implication is that co-planting Ricinus communis with legumes like Medicago sativa can improve growth and heavy metal uptake in Cd/Zn-contaminated soils, especially when the system is designed to reduce competitive stress and alter soil chemistry [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4]. The strongest evidence points to a facilitative effect: M. sativa increases R. communis height, biomass, and Cd/Zn uptake, while reducing heavy-metal stress [N3-F3]. However, the evidence also shows that Cd and Zn can reduce growth, chlorophyll, and photosynthesis, and that metal interactions can be antagonistic or synergistic depending on concentration [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4]. This means that co-planting is likely most effective in moderate contamination contexts and when soil amendments are used to optimize metal bioavailability [N2-F2][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2].

### Bottom line

In summary, the evidence supports a nuanced answer: **co-planting Ricinus communis with Medicago sativa improves growth and enhances Cd/Zn uptake in Cd/Zn-contaminated soils, but the effect depends on soil contamination levels, co-planting design, and amendments** [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2]. Legumes appear to mainly facilitate Ricinus through improved nutrient availability and soil chemistry rather than through dominant allelopathy, while Cd and Zn contamination harms growth, chlorophyll, and photosynthesis, with metal interactions often altering uptake and translocation [N5-R4][N5-R2][N5-R5][N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4]. The clearest direct evidence is that M. sativa can significantly increase height, biomass, and Cd/Zn uptake in R. communis, making it a promising co-planting partner for phytoremediation [N3-F3].
